item.research_question: Will trace interstitial impurities (oxygen and nitrogen) in Ti-V-Nb-Ta refractory high-entropy alloys continue to contribute positively to mechanical properties during long-term service, and will they affect phase stability or aid in phase segregation at in-service temperatures?
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting of high-purity elements, homogenization at 1200°C for 7 days followed by rapid cooling, and thermal aging at 700°C for durations of 1, 5, and 40 days.
item.test_conditions: Thermal aging at 700°C; nanoindentation with continuous stiffness measurement (CSM) at strain rate 0.05 s⁻¹; microstructural analysis via SEM, STEM, APT, EELS, and TKD.
key_findings: The homogenized Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy exhibits a hardness of 5.05 GPa, which decreases to 4.22 GPa after 40 days of aging at 700°C, representing a 16% reduction.
Trace interstitials in the matrix decrease from 1.12 to 1.3 at % in the 1-day aged sample to 0.56 to 0.64 at % in the 40-day aged sample.
Intragranular precipitates form with a volume fraction of approximately 3% after 40 days of aging.
The precipitates are identified as α-Ti phase containing 73.7 at % Ti, 18.3 at % O, and 5.88 at % N.
The calculated lattice distortion parameter (δ) decreases by approximately 17.6% when oxygen content drops from 1.2 at % to 0.6 at %.
Precipitates with a 3% volume fraction contribute only 217.48 MPa (5.15%) to the overall nanoindentation hardness.
Precipitate-free zones (PFZs) of approximately 3 μm width form adjacent to grain boundaries due to solute depletion.
The precipitates obey the Burgers orientation relationship: (0002)HCP ǁ {110}BCC and [112¯0]HCP ǁ <111>BCC.
item.mechanism: Trace interstitials (O and N) initially provide solid solution strengthening; upon aging, they partition to form α-Ti precipitates, depleting the matrix of these interstitials. This depletion reduces lattice distortions and solid solution strengthening, causing softening that outweighs the minimal hardening contribution from the 3% volume fraction of precipitates.
item.limitations: The study notes that quantifying solid solution strengthening in HEAs is challenging due to the inability to distinguish between solvent and solute atoms, and that the theoretical hardening calculations assume equal volume fractions for different precipitate morphologies.
item.future_work: The authors suggest exploring ways to strike a dynamic balance between hardening from aging precipitates and softening from reduced solid solution strengthening, and emphasize the need to better control oxygen and nitrogen levels during processing for industrial applications.
quotes: Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging.
The hardness of the 40-day aged sample, TiVNbTa-4, decreased by approximately 16% relative to the as-homogenized state, dropping to 4.22 GPa.
